doc.title: Albert Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 24, 1997

title: Refusing to define himself by political labels; American identity and Air Force years
summary: Murray declines to discuss how black Americans define themselves, calling it political confusion, and says he defines himself as an American. He recalls being a college teacher before being drafted in World War II.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: I’d prefer not to talk about that. I think it’s a lot of confusion about that that’s based on political maneuvering and has very little to do with an actual historic basis for definition. The stuff I’m interested in, defining my role as an American and the ways that the idiom that I grew up in add up to a definition of American character. But I don’t see any particular value in discussing what most people do because they get their images from sociology, from political strategy and stuff like this, more propaganda and stuff. It’s not very relevant. I just find it boring and confusing and all of this is counterproductive. It works against what their objectives are. Because I don’t see but one objective, and that’s to enjoy all of your birthright as an American. And that means achieving a synthesis of the most valuable and useful aspects of the American proposition, American culture and whatnot. And all Americans have problems of one sort or another, but they have individual personalities and individual goals and so forth, and you simply have to deal

with what the problems are. And I feel it’s literature, and so I’m interested in adequate images of the American experience and I assume the responsibility or part of the responsibility for the leadership of America in the world in terms of the human proposition that should be the basis of twentieth century living and I’ve spent quite a part of the twentieth century, eighty years of American life and all, and I’ve been a student of American culture and so forth, and I find that you know political formulations and things like that are not very, very useful, they’re propaganda, except they’re useful in a negative sense. They can get people mis-definitions of what they’re about and they forget to deal with themselves as human beings and they deal with themselves as abstractions from not life as data but ideological approaches which have to do with vested interests in certain aspects of American life.
When you were in your Air Force career, in your Air Force days, did you have aspirations to be a writer at that time also?

Oh yeah, I had been a college teacher before I was in the Air Force. I was drafted into the service and I had to do my time, during World War II, but I had already finished college and I was involved with literature. This was just another experience to me. But I had no basic images about being efficient, as I’d been taught to be in school. And I went to school from primary grade through high school and Mobile College Training School on the outskirts of Mobile. And it was geared to making responsible American citizens. That’s what it was about. And deal with whatever problems — it’s just like you have the general problems then you have individual, personal problems. And ultimately you deal with the problems that are personal to you, and you want to see what you can do about it, how far your abilities can take you, and that type of thing. That’s what I was always about.
